rounds.description: The round had a mix of technical and aptitude questions, with a total duration of about 90 minutes. It was a proctored test and divided into three sections: Aptitude, DSA, and SQL. All the questions were MCQ-based, so no actual coding was required.

rounds.name: Technical Interview I
rounds.description: There were two interviewers, and the interview began with a quick introduction where I had to talk about myself and my general hobbies. After that, they asked me about the programming languages I was comfortable with, and I said Python. From there, the discussion moved to OOPs concepts in Python. They asked me to share my screen and write a simple Car class with a few objects. Then they followed it up with questions on types of constructors and some magic methods I had used. They specifically asked about the use of __new__ and __call__ methods. Next, I got a string parsing question where I had to convert data into a list of dictionaries. The problem was straightforward, and I felt communication skills played a big role in explaining my thought process clearly. They also gave me a SQL question where I had to calculate the average ratings for a movie using two tables with joins. After that, there was a question on data warehousing concepts, which I wasn’t familiar with and I straight away said I dont know it. The interview wrapped up with a few questions about BlackRock as a company and why I was interested in working there.

rounds.name: Technical Interview II
rounds.description: This round had one senior interviewer who handled all the questions. He began with a quick introduction and even asked me to recall who had taken my Round 1, which I honestly couldn’t remember. Next, he went through all the projects from my resume and asked about the tech stack used. Since the role was for Data Engineering and most of my projects were in ML/Data Science, he wanted to know why I still felt I was a good fit. After that, he asked me how to store a polynomial and gave around 5–6 SQL queries verbally. I requested to share my screen and solve them on notepad, and he was fine with that. He then moved on to questions about RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) and asked if I was comfortable with it. Towards the end, the questions shifted to my daily use of AI, and he wrapped up by asking a thought-provoking one: “Why hire people when AI can already generate code?”

rounds.name: Temporary Round
rounds.description: On the interview day, i.e., 28 Aug, all results were already announced to the TPO. However, an AI copy-case incident happened during our interview rounds. The company caught some candidates using AI, which was very clearly evident to them. So, they decided to cancel the recruitment from SPIT. We all were tensed and anxious because, due to some candidates, everybody would have to suffer. So, the next day, Sikka Sir called 10 students for the next round, and Sikka Sir took an HR kind-of interview of us. Later, they discussed the copy-case incident and how they convinced the company not to cancel recruitment from SPIT, as BlackRock was visiting SPIT for the first time. After a stressful situation, Sikka Sir finally announced the names of the selected candidates, and we were very happy. The ones who copied using AI were straightaway rejected from the process.

tips.text: Placement preparation should start 3–4 months prior to the placement season. You can do it during your 5th semester. Preparing 1 month before placements will create huge pressure and stress. You will get no time to learn before OA or Interview Day. Ultimately, it depends on you how you manage your time.

If preparing for non-tech, do not fully rely on non-tech roles, as only 10% of roles are non-tech and 90% of jobs on our campus are tech roles (a mix of SDE and data roles). Always have a backup and prepare for the tech side by side.

Practice DSA and Aptitude and be well-versed before the placement season begins. It cannot be done one night prior or one week prior. And DSA & Aptitude done one night prior cannot help you clear OAs easily.
Once the OA-related part is cleared, focus on practicing for interviews. Try to give mocks to friends or try to improve communication skills in front of a mirror.

Prepare an approximate 2–3 minute introduction talking about your academics, internship/work experience details (showing its significance and what impactful work you have done), academic achievements (if any), and your interest in the role offered. This is the starting punch in which the interviewer understands you as a whole, analyzes the candidate, and prepares the next consecutive questions.
Always have a smile on your face and try to connect with the interviewer instead of just answering questions like a robot. Do not panic or be nervous, try to handle the situation.

Always ask effective questions to the interviewer at the end. Frame questions that can impress the interviewer and leave a lasting impression. Asking questions also shows that you are curious about the company. Do not ask vague or very basic questions.
Be very well-versed with the projects you prepare or put in your resume. You can expect deep questions about them. Diversify your projects, which will help you apply for various roles.

Usually, people say “do not compare yourself with others,” and that’s true—comparing yourself with others will always put you under stress and pressure. But what I would suggest is just keep a short analysis of your competitions, so that you know you need to perform better to clear tests & interviews.

Balance your preparation. Do not focus on only one skill. For eg. Do not do ONLY DSA & no Dev and Similarly do not do ONLY Dev & no DSA. Balance both things, plus additional CS Fundamentals and AIML concepts.

Do not get depressed by rejections. Rejection is a part of placements, and every rejection gives a learning. You should not give up and should keep trying again and again. Switch ON your beast mode and never settle until it is achieved. Trust on God’s plan. Even God takes our exam before giving results.

Always remember, placement is the joint result of hard work and luck. Luck is not in our control, but hard work is in our control. And Hard work increases the probability of Luck favouring you. You need to put in all your efforts to stand out from the crowd. AND if you are lazy and unambitious, then trust me you are already behind in the race.

Decide what you want to pursue Tech or Non tech. Tech people need not worry much because there will be a greater number of opportunities. But for Non tech people, kindly note that opportunities for Non tech are fewer and limited. So if preparing for Non Tech, then also prepare for Tech side by side as a backup.
The only thing you can do is be an ideal person who has knowledge of all skills and be ready for every kind of job.
Copying can be very risky. If found, you might not be able to sit for next 2-3 companies (which may be good companies).

Students with ONLY DSA skills were unable to answer web development questions in interviews, and students with ONLY development skills were unable to answer DSA questions in interviews. You need to prepare both.
Communication skills matter most in interviews and GDs. Even if you are intelligent but unable to convey your answers, you might not move forward.

You might see your friends or peers getting placed, but you should not take that as depression. Depression will slow down your productivity and willingness. Instead, you should learn from your mistakes, learn from your peers, put in more efforts, do not give up and achieve your goal.
Check your resume score on – resumeworded site. Try to keep above 65-70. It has limited no. of attempts, so use attempts wisely.

rounds.name: Online Assessment
rounds.description: This round was conducted on E-litmus platform and was proctored. It consisted on mainly 3 sections and all were of objective type(mcqs): 1. Logical reasoning,verbal reasoning,aptitude 2. Coding / algorithms 3. DBMS and SQL. This was of 90 minutes, but each section and subsection had its own time limit set. There were 4 subsections in 1st section, like verbal reasoning, logical reasoning, quantitative aptitude, and assertion reasoning type. All these subsections were easy to solve but lengthy, especially the quantitative aptitude one. Each sub section had its own time limit and navigation in subsection was not allowed, so had to carefully answer or leave the question. The questions were of cat-type basic aptitude and english questions, like speed and time, height and distance, work and efficiency, upstream and downstream, profit and loss, missing number or wrong number in the sequence. The 2nd section had flowchart type questions based on an algorithm or a scenario like lottery system, shopping mart. It had 4-5 questions based on each scenario, so had 4-5 such scenarios and each flowchart had a missing box to fill for that algorithm. There were some loops based mathematical coding questions as well, like to test the divisibility by 17 , what should be the main line :- first n-1 digits - 5* last digit should be divisible by 17. Then there were lengthy loop questions to calculate some mathematical sequences, like agp, gp, sum of squares. The 3rd section was of dbms and sql and had queries and database concepts like normalization, acid properties. Major questions were output type questions to the queries, like sysdate from dual, to_char function, and many more based on dual.

tips.text: In the OA, try not to spend more time on just 1 question, as it was very much time bound, especially the flowchart questions and quantitative aptitude.
confidence is a huge part of the game.
The interviewers valued direct and clear answers, and how you present your thought process seems just as important as the final solution.
They almost always threw in a couple of really tricky questions that felt designed to see how you handle pressure.
Honestly, getting through one of those tough problems gives you a major boost and makes the rest of the interview feel much more manageable.
even for your weakest subjects, try to have at least a basic, 30% level of understanding. It’s far better than being caught completely off guard.
interviewers want to see that you can think about the entire system, not just the code you wrote.
First, only list projects you are 100% confident you can defend, because they will ask tough, detailed questions.
Second, be careful about listing an outlier tech stack. If one project uses a technology that doesn't fit the rest of your story, interviewers will zoom in on it.
Your projects should highlight your strengths, not create traps.
know your strengths, strategically cover your weaknesses, and always be ready to explain your thinking with confidence.

rounds.name: Technical Interview Round 1
rounds.description: The first interview round began with a polite greeting and a brief self-introduction, where I highlighted my academic background, project work, and any relevant experiences. The interviewer then asked me to explain my projects in detail, focusing on the technologies used, the challenges faced, and the outcomes. I was also asked about my work experience, hobbies, and the skills I had gained from practical exposure. From there, the discussion moved to technical fundamentals, where I was asked about the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming and to name the programming languages I was most comfortable with. The interviewer also touched on role-fit and motivation questions, such as why I wanted to join BlackRock. I answered honestly, focusing on my interest in working with a global firm known for innovation and technology in finance. When asked about my knowledge of finance, I admitted that I did not have sufficient background but emphasized my willingness and eagerness to learn, which the interviewer seemed to appreciate. Toward the end, I was given the opportunity to ask a question, and I inquired about his routine and experience at BlackRock, which led to a more casual and insightful exchange.

rounds.name: Technical Interview Round 2
rounds.description: The second interview round was more project-focused and technical in nature. The interviewer began by asking me to choose one project that I would like to deep dive into. Once I selected the project, she asked detailed questions about its architecture, schema design, and the reasoning behind my technical choices. A key discussion point was on database design, where she asked me to compare SQL vs. NoSQL and explain which one I preferred in different scenarios. I elaborated on aspects like structured vs. unstructured data, scalability, and consistency, while also discussing how collections, documents, and sub-collections work in NoSQL databases. The interviewer then shifted the conversation toward financial awareness, asking how I keep myself updated with current financial situations. I responded by mentioning sources like financial news portals, online articles, and business publications, while also admitting I was still in the process of building deeper financial knowledge. Moving further, I was asked data analysis-oriented questions such as how I handled datasets in my projects, what tools I used, and importantly, whether I had deployed my work or kept it at an experimental stage. I clarified the scope of deployment in my projects and described my exposure to end-to-end development.

tips.text: When attempting the test, it is advisable to start with the section you are most confident in. Prioritizing technical MCQs and SQL questions can be beneficial, as securing accuracy in these areas helps maximize your score. If aptitude is not your strong suit, it is better to attempt that section at the end. This approach ensures that you focus first on questions where you are more likely to score, while managing time effectively across all sections.
If you don’t know the exact answer, keep communicating and explaining your thought process. Interviewers value your problem-solving approach as much as, or even more than, the final solution.
Always carry a smile and maintain a confident, positive demeanor throughout the interaction — it goes a long way in leaving a lasting impression.
Don’t lose confidence even if you face multiple rejections.
Even if you feel others less deserving are getting placed, remember that your journey is unique.
Stay confident and keep a smile throughout your interview. It creates a positive impression and shows your enthusiasm.

Always interact with the interviewers. Don’t stay quiet — even if you don’t know the exact answer, explain your thought process. Many times, they are more interested in how you approach the problem rather than just the final solution.
Practice explaining your projects clearly in bullet points (features, technologies, and real-world impact). This not only shows clarity but also highlights your problem-solving ability.
Know your resume inside out. HR and technical rounds can both heavily focus on what you’ve mentioned, so be prepared to discuss every detail confidently.
Prepare both technical and behavioral aspects. While DSA and technical knowledge are crucial, soft skills, communication, and genuine interest in the company matter equally.
Ask questions at the end. Always have 2–3 role- or company-related questions ready. This shows curiosity and genuine interest in the company.
Be consistent in preparation. Whether it’s aptitude, SQL, or programming, practicing regularly (LeetCode, mock tests, etc.) makes a big difference.
Network smartly. Connect with seniors, peers, or professionals on LinkedIn to get insights into the process. Sometimes even small tips can give you an edge.
And most importantly, trust the process. If one door closes, another one will open with an even better opportunity.

tips.text: Having a proper resume format (Jake's preferably) and one good project with unique features(Can be Major project) along with a couple of basic personal projects is sufficient to make your resume get shortlisted in campus placements. Make sure to write the project description in the form of pointers(the various features). Also, don't completely rely on gpt instead list down in your own words and refine it using gpt. Try to keep the project that sells more at the top.

YOU NEED TO HAVE TRUST IN YOURSELF AND IN YOUR PREPARATION. This doesn’t mean you have always prepared all the topics completely and have an overconfident attitude.Instead, you are well aware of what all you have prepared and what not and need to own that truth. Enjoy the test when the time comes. Breathe and take it slow , keep your mind focused in the present! THE MOST IMP THING: PLEASE PREPARE APTITUDE (Quants,LR,everything) properly from Indiabix.
Always remember to give examples!
Remember to be confident in what you explain and always keep talking!
It is a good practice to talk about each and every line of code on what you are doing.
First of all be clear on your motto, mine was-To get placed in a good company which can help me kickstart my career and offer growth opportunities.

Start early - This might be the only fruitful decision which determines how smooth your placement journey will be. I learned it the hard way. I started late but turns out I was capable enough to survive.Don’t get discouraged if you start late.

Be aware and plan out things- Always list down or atleast be aware of what you need to prepare.Initially I did not prepare the Core subjects- DBMS>OS>CCN. Later it becomes tough to cope up with extra preparation.

Focus on Aptitude preparation - You’ll think its easy, but there may be 30 people better than you always! I learned after failing a lot of aptitude tests. In the end, I significantly improved and had more faith in myself for the first time than my best friends had in me lol :)

Reach out to seniors who got placed last year just before any company process starts to get to know about their personal experience/ about the company and the roles. Also, If there is any company which is new, reach out on LinkedIn to random seniors(not necessarily from your college).People are always ready to help.This helped me for a couple of interviews.

Look up on failures and rejections and keep on telling yourself, there is a better opportunity waiting for you in the future which would be worth cracking and you’ll savor that moment. Also, learn from them and retrospect on what went wrong exactly and iteratively improve yourself on those parts.

these interview experiences are useful for you to get to know about some quirky/unusual questions. But remember these are just memoirs of the ones who slayed and everything went smooth for them during the process. So don’t completely rely on past experiences. For eg: If you come across a topic asked, try to learn about 5 more topics related to it and in detail. This preparation depth will matter as change in the job market is exponential in nature due to drastic developments in AI.
